evidence:
tls.lisp:371-375: ";; ... a larger one is reported absent (so ACL2 refuses it by name) rather than copied."
tls.lisp:383-385: `(if (or (not (integerp count)) (<= count 0) (> count +fnn-tls-max-fact-octets+) (sb-alien:null-alien data)) nil ...)`
books/tls-reload.lisp:307: `(cond ((null octets) nil) ...` (no names, not :malformed). fn-tlsr-start-decide accepts when names are not :malformed.
fix: Return a distinct marker for an unreadable or oversized extension (for example :unreadable) that fn-tlsr-san-names maps to :malformed. Otherwise fix the comment to say that an oversized SAN counts as no names.
reviewer: The tls.lisp:371-374 comment says an oversize SAN is 'reported absent (so ACL2 refuses it by name)'. fnn-tls-asn1-octets (383-386) returns NIL for count > 65536 or a null data pointer. fn-tlsr-san-names (books/tls-reload.lisp:307) maps NIL to no names, not :malformed, and the start decide (around line 460) only refuses :malformed. So a SAN over 64 KiB is accepted with an empty name set, and the comment does not match the code. Reaching this needs an operator-supplied certificate with a SAN extension over 64 KiB, which is practically never seen.
scenario: A certificate whose SAN extension is over 64 KiB, or whose ASN1 data pointer is NULL, gives san=NIL, which is exactly the 'no SAN' observation. `run` accepts it with an empty name set and the served line reports no names. A later reload then has an empty served-name set, so its names-dropped check protects nothing. 'Unreadable' and 'absent' are collapsed into one outcome, which contradicts the comment.
title: Comment says an oversize subjectAltName is refused by name, but absent is read as 'no names' and accepted
